Destroying the Ashoka Grove

Stories from the Ramayana

Destroying the Ashoka Grove

Hanuman makes a way to meet Ravana

In everyday English — Sundara Kanda, sargas 41–46

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story is made to be told. Read slowly, as if you are sitting with everyone at home.

This book is a hero's tale. Hanuman is alone — and the whole army of Lanka stands before him. Where the plan is made, read slowly; where the fighting comes, quicken your voice — but never shout.

The yellow boxes hold the characters' own words. Change your voice a little as you speak them — Hanuman thundering, Ravana furious, the rakshasis frightened.

(Purple hints) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

The green box at the end of each part — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask questions. Let the listeners speak.

The main story of this book is Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda, sargas 41–46 — the destruction of the Ashoka grove. Hanuman has already met Sita — now he wants to meet Ravana. Anything more you may want to know is given separately at the end, in Where This Story Comes From.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Hanuman — son of the Wind, minister of Sugriva, messenger of Rama. A powerful vanara, light golden-brown fur, long tail, gentle devoted face, saffron dhoti. The hero of this book.

Sita — held captive in the Ashoka grove. Wheat-gold skin, long black braid with white jasmine flowers, small gold jhumka earrings, a thin gold nose-ring on her left nostril, a single pale saree, no crown. Hanuman spares the very corner where she sits.

Ravana — king of Lanka. Tall, dark-complexioned, black moustache, tall golden crown, a single head, royal robes.

Prahasta — Ravana's chief minister. His son Jambumali and his seven sons appear in this story.

The Kinkaras — a troop of Ravana's soldiers — eighty thousand warriors, said to be as strong as Ravana himself.

Jambumali — son of Prahasta, a young warrior, master of the chariot and the bow.

Prahasta's seven sons — the minister's seven sons, with chariots and a great army.

The five generals — Virupaksha, Yupaksha, Durdhara, Praghasa and Bhasakarna — five great generals of Ravana's army.

1 · Hanuman's Plan · · HANUMAN'S PLAN

Hanuman sat on a tree in the Ashoka grove, thinking. He had met Sita — given her the crest-jewel, taken her message. One part of the work was done.

But one task remained — to meet Ravana. Hanuman wanted to see Ravana — his army, his strength, his palace — all with his own eyes.

He thought — “How shall I reach Ravana? He will not summon me. So I must do something that makes him summon me.”

He looked down — the Ashoka grove — the grove dearest to Ravana. Full of flowers, full of fruit, with beautiful pavilions.

Hanuman decided — “I will wreck this grove — but I will not touch the corner where Sita sits.”

“When Ravana hears that his beloved grove is wrecked — he will send an army to catch me — and I will reach his presence.”

Hanuman grew his body huge — huge as a mountain — and looked toward the grove. Now he was ready.

Pause and think — Hanuman wants to meet Ravana — but he does not go quietly, he goes with a noise. Is making a noise sometimes the right way? And is it right to break something someone loves, for the sake of a plan?

2 · The Grove Is Wrecked · · THE GROVE IS WRECKED

Hanuman seized a tree with both hands — and tore it out by the roots! The tree fell to the earth — flowers scattered, fruit rolled away.

Then a second tree — then a third. Hanuman tore up trees, smashed pavilions, churned the ponds. Birds screamed and flew into the sky.

The grove — which a little while ago had looked like heaven — now lay in ruins. Broken branches, scattered flowers, overturned pavilions.

But one corner remained untouched — the very corner where Sita sat beneath the Ashoka tree. Hanuman did not even glance that way.

The rakshasis guarding the grove ran screaming — “The grove is wrecked! A vanara has come — he is breaking everything!”

Hanuman roared — “I am Rama's messenger!” — and went and stood by the great archway.

Pause and think — Hanuman wrecked the grove — but he spared Sita's corner. Is that the right use of strength — to stop exactly where the innocent sit? And was Hanuman's roar a threat — or a message?

3 · The Kinkaras · · THE KINKARAS

◆ ◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it speaks of battle and killing. Elders, please read it gently.

The rakshasis ran to Ravana — “Great king! The Ashoka grove is wrecked! A mighty vanara has come — he is tearing up trees and smashing pavilions!”

Ravana turned red with rage. He ordered — “Go — send the Kinkaras! Eighty thousand warriors — go and bring that vanara to me!”

The Kinkaras — Ravana's most trusted soldiers — ran toward the grove with spears, swords and maces. Eighty thousand — a whole army!

Hanuman tore out the great iron door-bar — the heavy latch of the gate. That became his weapon.

Then what happened was war. Hanuman swung the bar — and the Kinkaras fell one by one. Eighty thousand warriors — and a single vanara. At last silence fell over the grove.

Hanuman climbed the archway again — and waited for what would come next.

Pause and think — Eighty thousand against a single Hanuman — is that bravery — or madness? And when one person fights so many alone — is his strength in his body — or in his mind?

4 · The Sanctuary · · THE SANCTUARY

◆ ◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it speaks of battle and killing. Elders, please read it gently.

Hanuman thought — “Ravana will send more armies. But why should I wait here? I want to see more of his strength.”

Near the grove stood a Chaitya-prasada — the sacred sanctuary of the guardian deity of the ogres. Guards stood at its door.

Hanuman climbed it. The guards tried to stop him — but Hanuman defeated them — and tore out a great pillar of the sanctuary.

Fire came from the whirling pillar — and the sanctuary began to burn. Hanuman roared — so loudly that Lanka shook — “Victory to Rama!”

That roar was heard in Ravana's palace — and Ravana's rage grew greater still.

Pause and think — Hanuman broke the ogres' sacred sanctuary — was that only war — or a message to Ravana? And the roar of “Victory to Rama” — was that only a sound — or is Rama's name itself Hanuman's strength?

5 · Jambumali · · JAMBUMALI

◆ ◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it speaks of battle and killing. Elders, please read it gently.

Ravana called his minister Prahasta — “Who will go? Who will catch that vanara?”

Prahasta said — “Great king, my son Jambumali will go. He is young, he is brave, he is master of the bow.”

Jambumali came riding a chariot — a great chariot, swift horses, a great bow. He stood before Hanuman — and shot his arrows.

A fierce fight followed. Jambumali's arrows filled the sky — but Hanuman dodged them — leaping, ducking.

At last Hanuman swung that same iron bar — and Jambumali fell. Prahasta's son — Ravana's trusted warrior — was killed.

When Ravana heard this — his face went pale. Now he was beginning to understand — this was no ordinary vanara.

Pause and think — Jambumali was young and brave — and he went at his father's word. Was his defeat his own failing — or Hanuman's strength? And when someone fights a greater enemy — is even defeat a kind of bravery?

6 · Prahasta's Seven Sons · · PRAHASTA'S SEVEN SONS

◆ ◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it speaks of battle and killing. Elders, please read it gently.

Ravana ordered again — “Go — all seven sons of Prahasta! On chariots, with a great army — bring that vanara to me!”

The seven brothers came — seven chariots, seven bows, and a great army with them. They were swift as fire — and skilled with the bow.

Hanuman broke their arrows as if in play — now with his hand, now by leaping. Then he tore up a great tree — and swung it at the seven chariots.

The seven brothers — one by one — fell. Their army too fled.

Hanuman climbed the archway again — and stood there waiting for Ravana's next move.

Pause and think — Seven brothers came together — and fell one by one. Are numbers alone strength? And why does Hanuman climb back onto the archway every time — has that place become his post?

7 · The Five Generals · · THE FIVE GENERALS

◆ ◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it speaks of battle and killing. Elders, please read it gently.

Ravana now called his five great generals — Virupaksha, Yupaksha, Durdhara, Praghasa and Bhasakarna. These were the greatest names in Lanka's army.

Ravana said — “Go — bring that vanara to me. Bring him alive — I want to ask him who he is.”

The five generals came — on chariots, on an elephant, raining arrows. Their arrows covered the sky.

Hanuman broke their arrows. Then he leapt onto one general's chariot — and smashed it to pieces.

Then he tore up a mighty teak tree — and struck down two generals with it. The rest he struck down with great boulders.

The five generals — the five great names of Lanka — fell one by one. Hanuman returned to the archway.

Pause and think — Five generals — Lanka's greatest names — and Hanuman alone. Is a name itself strength? And why does Hanuman lift trees and boulders — does he have no weapon — or is nature itself his weapon?

8 · Hanuman on the Archway · · HANUMAN ON THE ARCHWAY

Evening was falling. The Ashoka grove lay in ruins — trees broken, pavilions fallen, flowers scattered.

And on the archway — the great gate of the grove — stood Hanuman. Alone. Tired — but unmoved.

Ravana had sent so far — eighty thousand Kinkaras, Jambumali, Prahasta's seven sons, five generals — and all had been defeated.

Hanuman roared again — “Victory to Rama!” — and looked toward Lanka. He knew — now Ravana himself would have to do something.

And Ravana — in his palace — was thinking. His army was losing. Now he was thinking of sending his own son — his young son Aksha.

But that story — is the next book's.

Pause and think — Hanuman stands alone on the archway — and all of Lanka watches him. Can one person alone hold back a whole army? And when all are defeated — what does a king do — does he send his own son?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main source

The main story of this book is Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda, sargas 41–46 — the destruction of the Ashoka grove.

Hanuman's plan and the wrecking of the grove — sarga 41

The decision to wreck the grove in order to meet Ravana; wrecking the whole grove except the part where Sita sits; tearing up trees, smashing pavilions, birds flying away — this is in sarga 41.

The Kinkaras — sarga 42

The rakshasis running to Ravana; Ravana sending eighty thousand Kinkaras; Hanuman killing them with the heavy iron door-bar of the gate — this is in sarga 42.

The sanctuary — sarga 43

Climbing the sanctuary sacred to the guardian deity of the ogres; killing the guards posted there; tearing out a gold-decorated pillar; burning the sanctuary; roaring Rama's name — this is in sarga 43.

Jambumali — sarga 44

Ravana sending Jambumali, son of Prahasta; the fierce fight on the chariot; Hanuman killing him with the same iron bar — this is in sarga 44.

Prahasta's seven sons — sarga 45

Ravana sending the seven sons of his minister Prahasta with chariots and a great army; Hanuman breaking their arrows and killing them; Hanuman climbing the archway again — this is in sarga 45.

The five generals — sarga 46

Ravana sending five generals — Virupaksha, Yupaksha, Durdhara, Praghasa and Bhasakarna; Hanuman breaking their arrows, leaping on a chariot and smashing it, killing two with a teak tree and the rest with boulders; Hanuman returning to the archway — this is in sarga 46.

About the pictures

This book's pictures show the fighting — but never death, a body, or blood. The pictures show the moment before the fight — Hanuman's stand, the armies arriving, the ruined grove. The killing is told only in words.

What happens next

Ravana is now thinking of sending his young son Aksha — and after him his eldest son Indrajit. Aksha's story is the next book of this series.
